[00:00] Jordan (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Jordan from Redwood Inference. with me is Maya, our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?

[00:13] Jordan: awesome. quick agenda — run through what you folks are trying to accomplish, current stack, then we cover options: self-serve hosted API quickstart, reserved/dedicated pools, or private (VPC/on-prem) and then outline pilot next steps. sound OK?
[00:26] Marcus (Infra): yep good.
[00:28] Priya: perfect. so to start, our team spun up a small internal prototype using a fine-tuned open LLM on k8s, right now it's erratic at scale and costs are spiking, latency is variable. we need better predictability and also we have security constraints — some data must remain in region and we need audit logs.
[00:44] Maya (SE): that makes sense. can you share a bit about volumes — qps and average sequence lengths? also do you have internal quantization or are you running fp16?
[00:54] Priya: for now it's small, 10-30 qps bursty, typical seq len ~ 128 tokens, but some prompts go to 512. model is a medium-sized decoder, we don't want to disclose full model name on this call.
[01:07] Jordan: totally. and timeline — are you looking to have pilot in next few weeks or months?
[01:11] Liam: pilot in next 3-4 weeks ideally, production in Q1. main success criteria: p95 latency under 350ms for common paths, cost per 1k tokens under our current budget threshold, and SOC2 gap closure for log retention and SSO.
[01:26] Maya: ok great. re: quickstart — our PLG/self-serve flow gets you to a first request in under an hour typically: sign up, SDK keys, run sample call. free credits can be applied for a prototype run; that covers basic smoke tests. TTFT for real traffic depends on model and batching settings but first token is usually sub-100ms on hosted endpoints for small models, though you'll see variance if seq len spikes.
[01:52] Marcus: hm sub-100ms first token, is that realistic for 128 token sequences?
[01:56] Maya: first token latency is mostly model compute + network. for 128 seq it's usually 60-120ms on our optimized hosted fleet for mid-size models; full response time scales linearly. with dedicated pools you can tighten p95 by reserving GPUs and setting pre-warmed kernels.
[02:12] Priya: what about KV cache and repeated calls for chat-like flows? that's where our metrics get weird.
[02:18] Maya: we have automatic KV cache on request paths that are route pinned, and continuous batching. caching reduces repeated prefix compute but you need to pin model versions and routes. on hosted the cache window is managed by us; on Dedicated/Private you can control retention.
[02:32] Jordan: quick clarification: when we say hosted vs dedicated — hosted is rapid self-serve with free credit trials, dedicated is reserved capacity for predictable throughput, private is VPC or on-prem for compliance and data residency.
[02:45] Liam: right, we care about data residency in EU and audit logs, also KMS integration for key control. do you support customer-managed keys?
[02:54] Maya: yes, for Private deployments we support KMS/HSM and customer-managed key integrations. For Dedicated we can integrate with cloud KMS with proper IAM. Hosted supports envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key in certain enterprise plans.
[03:08] Priya: what about SOC2 and SSO — do you have SOC2 Type II?
[03:12] Jordan: Redwood is SOC2 compliant and we have ISO-27001 in process, we will share the security pack. SSO SAML/SCIM is supported for enterprise accounts, RBAC and audit logs are available by default on Dedicated/Private.
[03:26] Marcus: perfect. another thing — we're doing A/B experiments on model variants, can we run canary rollouts?
[03:31] Maya: yes — rollouts and model versioning are first-class. you can do canaries, A/B, and automatic fallback to smaller models when latency SLOs are threatened.
[03:40] Liam: ok show of hands — how fast do you think we could get a pilot with, say, 2m tokens worth of traffic simulated?
[03:46] Jordan: if we do hosted quickstart with credits, you could simulate within a day. if you need Dedicated reserved pool it's a bit longer — provisioning and config might take 1-2 weeks. Private on-prem is obviously longer, a few weeks to months depending on networking.
[03:59] Priya: for our pilot we want to test worst-case prompts, 512 tokens plus some streaming flows. will the SDK handle streaming and function/tool calling?
[04:08] Maya: yes we support streaming, tool-calling, structured output, and function-calling paradigms. small note — sometimes the auto-transcripts show product names differently; our console name is Redwood Console, but folks often say "Redwood Dashboard" which is the same.
[04:22] Liam: hah, good to know. now on costs — if we move to Dedicated, what's the commitment and are there burst options?
[04:29] Jordan: Dedicated is based on reserved GPU capacity, monthly or annual commits. you get predictable throughput and lower per-token unit costs. we offer burst policies for occasional spikes; billing and overage terms are in the SOW.
[04:38] Marcus: how do you handle quantized models and mixed precision on the runtime? we currently use int8 quantization in prod.
[04:45] Maya: our runtime is quantization-friendly; we support int8 and mixed precision. we recommend a small quantization validation to check quality regression. Redwood Optimize (sometimes called Redwood Optimizer in notes) can recommend quantization profiles by workload.
[04:58] Priya: the team is worried about quality regressions with aggressive quantization — how do you guard for that?
[05:03] Maya: we do prompt-set tied evals and can run regression alerts. for pilots we normally run the customer's representative prompts and produce a quality delta report. that’s part of the micro-benchmarking we offered.
[05:15] Jordan: quick commercial note — we can grant free credits to run a pilot; typically the PLG path gives X credits (we'll detail in email). credits are intended for first-run testing and basic benchmarking, not sustained production traffic.
[05:28] Liam: that should be fine. for SSO/audit we need to see the compliance pack and the last pen test summary.
[05:33] Jordan: we'll send the security pack and SOC2 report.
[05:36] Priya: excellent. one more technical — network egress: if we use Private VPC mode, can we keep egress within our peered tenant?
[05:44] Maya: yes, Private supports customer VPC peering and you can keep traffic inside your cloud region, also supports on-prem air-gapped installs if required.
[05:53] Marcus: outstanding. for the benchmark, what metrics will you report?
[05:57] Maya: we'll report first-token latency distribution, p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, and memory/cpu utilization for the model variant. we'll include notes on batching and caching settings used.
[06:10] Priya: can you also surface how to tune batching and the tradeoffs? we want to avoid increasing p95 when enabling batching.

[06:29] Liam: timeline recap? we want pilot in ~3 weeks. what do you need from us to move forward?
[06:35] Jordan: ideal ask: you share 200-500 representative prompts, expected concurrency profile, and SLO targets. we'll spin up a quick hosted pilot with credits and Maya will run the micro-benchmark. after that, if results match your SLOs, we propose a short Dedicated pilot SOW.
[06:51] Priya: ok we'll collect inputs by next Wednesday.
[06:55] Jordan: perfect. any blockers around procurement or legal?
[06:58] Liam: procurement reviews standard enterprise contracts; we might need a few custom clauses for data residency. process takes 2-3 weeks typically.
[07:07] Jordan: noted, we'll prepare a clean SOW and flag data residency clauses.
[07:11] Marcus: question — do you provide streaming metrics for cost per token in the console?

[07:59] Priya: good. we'll likely want to keep private repo of models; how do you handle model registry and version control?
[08:05] Maya: we have a model catalog and versioning; for Private deployments you can host the registry. For hosted we manage the catalog but you can pin versions and upload via secure channel.
